newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - RWE makes new connections in German telecoms. [CORRECTED 13:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - RWE makes new connections in German telecoms. [CORRECTED 13:45 GMT]

text.p: RWE AG, in a surprise move, said on Wednesday it would ally with Veba AG and Cable & Wireless Plc to challenge monopoly Deutsche Telekom AG when Germany's telecoms market is deregulated in 1998.

Utility RWE pulled out of talks dating back to last winter on a partnership with Bavaria's Viag and British Telecom Plc, citing differences over strategy in plans to bid for Germany's planned E2 mobile phone network.
The switch marks a big realignment in the courtship between German utilities and international phone companies looking to tie in their infrastructure and know-how to build new networks.
RWE said in a statement it was "taking a new direction to enter the German telecommunications market."
Talks with Veba and C&W were in their final stages and an announcement was due later in the day after a supervisory board meeting, the statement added.
The announcement took share dealers by surprise and stock in all three companies initially jumped on the news, while British Telecom and Viag suffered setbacks.

RWE's common stock closed up 2.90 marks at 60.60 marks, while Veba rose 68 pfennigs to 81.53 marks. Viag tumbled 21 marks to 581 marks. In London, C&W rose initially before settling back to stand unchanged at 434p by 1130 GMT, while BT was off seven pence at 349.

RWE, BT and Viag last February announced plans to build a nationwide telephone network to start competing with Deutsche Telekom immediately after the opening up of the German market on January 1, 1998.
But industry sources said that a row between BT and RWE hit the plans to invest five billion marks ($3.3 billion) in the project by 2001.

In its statement RWE cited "differences in market positioning" over the planned E2 mobile network, Germany's fourth. The E2 licence will be awarded in February next year. The government is taking bids for the licence until October 15.
Industry sources told Reuters that RWE and BT had fallen out in part because RWE was seeking a majority stake in some joint subsidiaries.

They also said that RWE wanted to focus on the terrestrial telephone network, regarding likely investment costs of four billion marks to establish E2 as too expensive. BT wanted to put the E2 bid at the core of its strategy.
Although BT and Viag said they would soldier on with a joint bid for the E2 licence, with the departure of RWE they have lost the nationwide cover to back up their partnership.

BT said in London that it would seek new partners -- either on the infrastructure side or the equity side -- to pursue its German plans. It and Viag (corrects from "RWE") have called a joint news conference for Thursday at 0800 GMT to detail their plans.
"Cable will incur much lower start-up losses as RWE moves in to take its share." said Michael Hepburn, analyst at ABN Amro Hoare Govett. "The alliance is a definite positive for Cable & Wireless."
The deal is also bad news for British Telecom.
"It translates to increased capital expenditures and further earnings dilution if RWE is missing from the equation," Hepburn said.
Analysts speculated that British Telecom may now aim for a closer relationship with Thyssen, which is seeking a telecommunications partner and is a shareholder in the E-Plus mobile phone group.
There was also some speculation that RWE could take a stake in C&W. Veba already owns 10.5 percent of Cable & Wireless and they jointly own the German telecommunications venture Vebacom.
"The telecommunications strategy of Viag and BT will continue unchanged without the entry of RWE into the alliance," Viag said in a separate news release.
